title: Squared Deviations
story: A greenhouse sensor records how far each reading is from the ideal temperature. Too cold gives a negative number, too warm a positive one. The log is already sorted from lowest to highest, for example [-7, -3, 0, 2, 5].
The climate system cares about the size of each miss, and it punishes big misses more, so it uses the square of each deviation. It wants those costs sorted from smallest to largest.
task: Write squaredSorted(deviations). Return a new list with the square of every number, sorted from smallest to largest.
Aim for a single pass. The input is sorted; use that.
constraints: deviations is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: The squares in input order are 49, 9, 0, 4, 25. Sorted: 0, 4, 9, 25, 49. Notice the biggest squares came from the two ends of the input: -7 and 5.
Squares in order: 16, 1, 0, 9, 100. The largest, 100, comes from the right end. The next largest, 16, comes from the left end.

hints: Squaring the numbers breaks the sorted order. But where in the input do the largest squares come from?
The biggest square is always at one of the two ends: either the most negative number or the most positive one. The middle holds the numbers closest to zero.
So you can find the answer from largest to smallest. Compare the squares at the two ends, and the bigger one is the largest value still to place.
Use left and right pointers at the ends, and fill the result from the back. Each step, write the larger of the two end squares at the current back position and move that pointer inward.
bruteForce: Square every number, then sort the result. It is two lines of code and it is correct.
It costs O(n log n) because of the sort, and it ignores the fact that the input was already sorted. The sorted input is a gift: it tells you where the big values are.

walkthrough: The largest square is always at one end of the input, so build the answer from the largest down.
Trace [-7, -3, 0, 2, 5]. The result has 5 slots, filled from the back:
1. Ends are -7 and 5. 49 > 25, so slot 4 = 49. Move left to -3.
• Ends are -3 and 5. 9 < 25, so slot 3 = 25. Move right to 2.
• Ends are -3 and 2. 9 > 4, so slot 2 = 9. Move left to 0.
• Ends are 0 and 2. 0 < 4, so slot 1 = 4. Move right to 0.
Each step places exactly one value and moves exactly one pointer, so the loop runs n times.
solution.timeWhy: One loop that places one value per step.
solution.spaceWhy: The result list. Apart from it, only two pointers.
solution.takeaway: When a sorted input gets scrambled in a predictable way, look at the ends. Two pointers that start at the ends and fill the answer from the back is a common way to merge two sorted halves in one pass.
